stories.headline: Kenyan Cult Leader Paul Mackenzie Convicted of Manslaughter in 123 More Deaths
stories.summary:
A court in Mombasa, Kenya, on Friday convicted doomsday cult leader Paul Mackenzie of the manslaughter of 123 followers. He was found guilty of ordering adult followers to fast to death in Shakahola forest between January 2021 and September 2023. The court also convicted 29 others, including his wife, Rhoda Mumbua Maweu, while 60 defendants were acquitted.

Earlier this month Mackenzie was jailed for 200 years for the murder of 191 people, nearly all of them children, in the same mass killing. He was also convicted this week of assault, child cruelty, organised criminal activity and terrorism-related offences. Prosecutors described Friday's verdict as the final conviction in the cases against him, and said children were to die first, then women, then men, with Mackenzie last. Authorities arrested him in 2023 after more than 400 bodies were found in shallow graves.

Mackenzie pleaded not guilty, and one of his lawyers said he would appeal after sentencing. The Director of Public Prosecutions indicated it would appeal the acquittals of the 60 defendants. Witnesses testified that he preached against education and medicine and that opponents were beaten to death.

stories.headline: Trump to Attend Groundbreaking at Phoenix TSMC Chip Plant Amid Nvidia Turmoil
stories.summary:
President Trump will tour and deliver remarks at the groundbreaking of a Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Co. facility in Phoenix, a White House official told multiple outlets. The plant will manufacture semiconductors including chips for Nvidia. The visit highlights the administration's push to expand domestic chip production.

The event comes as Nvidia is in the spotlight over the ouster and reinstatement of CEO Jensen Huang, with Trump pushing for Huang's return. Bloomberg reported that two Chinese firms installed Nvidia's Blackwell chips in a Shanghai data center linked to Alice Huang, the woman whose extramarital affair with Huang is at the center of the controversy. Earlier reporting showed Trump holds millions of dollars in Nvidia stock and has called a pardon for Huang 'always an option'.

Supporters of the administration view domestic chip manufacturing as a strategic and economic priority. Critics, including Democratic strategists, have focused on the president's ties to Nvidia and his involvement in the company's leadership dispute. The exact date and details of the visit were not specified in the reports.

stories.headline: Trump Backs Iraqi Prime Minister's Push to Put Oil and Weapons Under State Control
stories.summary:
President Trump on Friday expressed support for Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's effort to assert state authority across Iraq. In a Truth Social post, Trump said, "We support Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi's efforts to assert state authority throughout Iraq, stop the smuggling of Iraqi oil, end corruption, and bring all weapons under the exclusive control of the state."

The endorsement centers on an anti-corruption campaign that includes consolidating the country's oil and weapons under government control. Bringing arms under exclusive state control would bear on armed factions operating outside official command, a sensitive issue as the United States is engaged in a war with Iran.

The statement is a notable foreign-policy signal from Washington about its preferred direction for Baghdad. Al Jazeera and the Washington Examiner both covered it. Details of any concrete US assistance or Iraqi implementation steps were not provided.

stories.headline: Canada's Supreme Court Upholds Quebec Ban on Religious Symbols for Public Servants
stories.summary:
Canada's Supreme Court on Friday upheld a Quebec law that bars public servants from wearing religious symbols at work. The ban applies to teachers and police officers, among others, and covers items such as hijabs and turbans. It remains in place following the ruling.

The law faced legal challenges from a range of groups, including female Muslim, Sikh and Catholic teachers. They argued it violated their fundamental rights. Civil liberties groups say the law is discriminatory and disproportionately targets Muslim women, and the decision is expected to upset them.

Supporters of the law in Quebec have defended it as an expression of the province's secular character and of its authority to set rules for public institutions. The ruling is seen as a test of Canadian unity, since it bears on the balance between provincial powers and individual rights protected under the national constitution.

The decision ends a lengthy legal fight over one of the most contested pieces of legislation in recent Canadian politics. It leaves the ban in force for public-sector workers across the province and is likely to shape debate over religious freedom and secularism in Canada.

stories.headline: Update: Trump Says Iran War Will End 'Sort of Whenever I Want It to Be'
stories.summary:
President Donald Trump said the war with Iran will be over "sort of whenever I want it to be," as the conflict stretches into its ninth month. He made the remarks while taking questions on the Thanksgiving holiday, suggesting he has the power to end the fighting at will. He also called soldiers at Mar-a-Lago alongside first lady Melania Trump.

The comments come as pushback against the war grows. Democrats have been weighing efforts to cut off funding for the conflict, though their next steps remain unclear. Supporters of the president have framed the military campaign as necessary to counter Iranian aggression and protect American forces and allies, while critics argue it lacks a defined endpoint and congressional authorization.

Iran's foreign minister, Abbas Araghchi, described a recent incident as "suspicious" and "a precooked recipe for war." Tehran has denied responsibility for several recent attacks, including a drone strike in Kuwait that killed two Italians.

The president's remarks offered no timeline or conditions for ending the conflict. They are likely to fuel debate in Congress over war powers and funding as lawmakers return from the holiday.

stories.headline: China Drives Biggest Stock Gain Since 2024 With Rare Midday Pledge of Market Support
stories.summary:
Chinese stocks posted their best day in more than two years after authorities issued a rare midday statement pledging support for markets. The unusual timing of the release from China's cabinet signaled urgency and sent equities sharply higher.

The statement stressed that the government would back market stability. Such midday announcements are uncommon in Chinese policymaking, which is why the reaction was so strong. It was the largest one-day gain since 2024.

The move comes amid trade tension, including proposed US tariff hikes that China, Japan and other partners have protested. Investors will watch whether the pledge is followed by concrete measures such as funding or regulatory steps.

Separately, senators from both parties say Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick faces pressure after revelations that Nvidia sold billions of dollars of high-tech chips to a Singapore-based company whose former senior executive, Alice Huang, is accused of being a Chinese spy.

stories.headline: Serbia's Student Movement Names Chemistry Professor Radomir Saicic as Presidential Candidate
stories.summary:
Serbia's student movement on Friday announced chemistry professor Radomir Saicic as its candidate for the early presidential election on Dec. 27. Saicic, 65, teaches organic chemistry at the University of Belgrade. He said it was time "to restore dignity to the post of the president" and promised to publicly explain his decisions.

The vote follows the student movement's defeat of former President Aleksandar Vucic's right-wing Serbian Progressive Party in an early parliamentary ballot on Oct. 25. Vucic resigned the presidency in September to pursue a failed bid for prime minister after 14 years of near-unchallenged rule. Analysts expect the party would likely lose to the Students List candidate, and Vucic has suggested it could boycott the vote.

The movement grew from two years of street protests that began after a train station canopy collapse in Novi Sad killed 16 people. Many blamed corruption and negligence in the renovation. Vucic has accused the winners of imposing "revolutionary terror," while detentions of officials and police suspected of abuses have surged.

The presidency is largely ceremonial, though Vucic concentrated power in it. It remains unclear which other candidates will enter the race.

stories.headline: Houthi Attacks on Saudi Arabia Surge Since July, Testing Kingdom's Security
stories.summary:
A BBC analysis of data from the Armed Conflict Location and Event Data Project (Acled) identified 274 Houthi attacks on Saudi Arabia between 1 July and 25 November. Most were intercepted, but at least 41 were not, and debris from some interceptions caused damage. Drones featured in almost two-thirds of the attacks and ballistic missiles in more than half. In the previous five months, Acled recorded just one Houthi attack on the country.

The escalation followed the collapse of an informal ceasefire in Yemen in July. The Iran-backed Houthis say they are retaliating for deadly Saudi air strikes in Yemen and for what they describe as a Saudi blockade of ports and airports in Houthi-controlled territory. The deadliest single incident was a strike on Riyadh's international airport on 10 October, which killed 13 people and injured more than 300, the worst attack on Saudi soil in years.

BBC reporters, granted rare permission to work in Riyadh, spoke to residents living under the threat. Majid, a 25-year-old Aramco engineer who was in the airport during the strike, described seeing injured and unconscious passengers and said, "The threat is real, but I will not let the Houthis make me feel unsafe in my own country." Yemeni civilians are also fleeing; one man who escaped Sanaa for Riyadh said families in Yemen are struggling to provide for their children.

The attacks carry wider regional weight as the Iran war continues and the kingdom, which has promoted an image of stability to attract investment, faces sustained strikes on its cities.

stories.headline: Update: Iran War: US Task Force Iron Gate Aims to Cut Tehran's Overland and Caspian Trade Routes
stories.summary:
U.S. Central Command announced earlier this month the creation of Task Force Iron Gate, a unit charged with disrupting the overland and Caspian Sea routes Iran has relied on since the U.S. naval blockade sealed its southern ports on the Persian Gulf and the Gulf of Oman. The announcement came amid reports that the blockade was leaky, including hundreds of trucks lining up at Iran's border crossing with Turkey and trade being rerouted north through the Caspian.

In a National Review commentary, Miad Maleki, a former senior Treasury sanctions official, and Behnam Ben Taleblu, both of the Foundation for Defense of Democracies, argue that the scramble is a turning point. In their view, Iran's overland efforts reveal the regime's remaining economic arteries, and Washington has now built the tool to cut them. This is an advocacy-oriented analysis from a hawkish think tank.

Critics of the administration's approach, including some outlets and lawmakers on the left, have questioned the strategy's cost and its open-ended nature. Democrats have said they plan to cut off funding for the war, though their next steps remain unclear. The piece reflects one side of a continuing debate over whether economic pressure can force Tehran to change course.

The effectiveness of the new task force will depend on cooperation from neighboring states such as Turkey and Caspian littoral countries, and on how Iran responds to further restrictions on its trade.

stories.headline: Hackers Breach US Air Force's Cloud One Computing Platform, Reuters Reports
stories.summary:
Hackers broke into the U.S. Air Force's main cloud computing platform, Cloud One, in recent weeks, according to a Reuters report citing three sources. The platform hosts sensitive personal and logistics data. The breach was discovered over the past month and caused disruption across the platform.

It is unclear who was behind the attack or how much data the intruders accessed. The incident is the latest in a string of cyber incidents and outages at government agencies, raising questions about the security of federal cloud systems.

The Air Force has not detailed the scope of the compromise in the reporting available. Further disclosures on attribution, the data affected and remediation are likely as officials and lawmakers press for answers.

stories.headline: Judge Pauses Order to Hand Over Seized 2020 Fulton County Ballots to Georgia Election Board
stories.summary:
A Fulton County, Georgia, judge has blocked her own order requiring that electronic copies of 2020 election ballots, seized by the FBI in a raid, be turned over to the Georgia State Election Board. Superior Court Judge Kelly Lee Ellerbe paused the order after county election officials filed a notice of appeal.

The ballots were taken in an FBI raid, and the dispute over who may access them continues to draw attention to the handling of 2020 election records. County officials are seeking appellate review before any copies are released.

Supporters of broader access argue that the state board has a legitimate oversight role, while critics view continued scrutiny of the 2020 vote as a politically motivated effort to relitigate a settled election. The appeal will determine whether and when the board receives the data.

stories.headline: EU Leaders Defer Long-Term Budget Talks After 12-Hour Summit Ends Without Deal
stories.summary:
European Union leaders have postponed negotiations on the bloc's 2028-34 budget after a 12-hour summit in Brussels on Thursday ended without agreement. Some members walked out, and talks will resume in December. The current proposal totals 1.582 trillion euros, including 140 billion euros to repay pandemic-era borrowing, and the European Council had proposed cutting spending by roughly 220 billion to 230 billion euros from the Commission's 2 trillion euro plan.

The divisions fell largely along national lines. France and Italy favor a higher-spending budget to support farming and regional development, while fiscally cautious countries led by Germany want to avoid ballooning debt. Four countries seeking restraint, including Denmark and Austria, left the negotiations after several hours. French President Emmanuel Macron said lowering long-term spending would be a strategic mistake. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz said there was new movement toward a smaller budget but added that we are not there yet, and confirmed no new round would be held Friday.

A proposed additional 45 billion euro loan to Ukraine, split between military and non-military funding, remains contested. Slovakia, the Czech Republic and Hungary object, but Merz said EU-wide agreement was a condition for approving the broader budget, adding that the Union comprises 27 member states, not 23 or 24. Bulgaria, which had opposed the plan, said it would back the non-military portion, a small sign of progress.

EU budgets require unanimity, so every member effectively holds a veto. Many governments want a deal before several high-stakes 2027 elections, including in France, where frontrunner Marine Le Pen condemned the talks as underhanded manoeuvring to thwart the will of French voters. She has pledged to sharply reduce French aid to Ukraine and EU contributions if elected.

stories.headline: Spain's Party Leaders Clash in Final Debate Before Sunday Election as Housing Dominates
stories.summary:
Spain's main party leaders made their last pitch to voters in a contentious televised debate on Thursday night, with the housing crisis at the center of discussion. Spaniards vote on Sunday, and polls suggest Socialist Prime Minister Pedro Sanchez will fail to extend his eight years in office. Sanchez called the snap election after Congress rejected his emergency housing reforms.

Alberto Nunez Feijoo of the conservative People's Party, which is narrowly projected to finish first, promised to build a million new homes. The PP is expected to need the support of Vox, polling third. If Vox enters government, it would be the first time the far right has held national power in Spain since the end of the Franco dictatorship. Vox leader Santiago Abascal said only his party cared about those in greatest housing need, while Ada Colau, who leads the Broad Front left coalition, called for taxing wealthy and exploitative landlords.

Sanchez defended his recent emergency measures to protect tenants and cap rent increases, rejecting criticism that he had failed to address the problem. The campaign has featured demonstrations in which protesters jangle house keys, sparked in September by the eviction, and later death in hospital, of an 87-year-old Madrid woman who could not afford a tripling of her rent. Valencia has seen the steepest rent rises among major cities, about 78 percent between 2020 and 2025 according to one university study.

stories.headline: Guinea-Bissau's Military Rulers Postpone Elections Until November 2028
stories.summary:
Guinea-Bissau's military government has postponed presidential and parliamentary elections, originally scheduled for December 6, by almost two years. Transitional President Gen Horta N'Tam announced in a decree that the votes will now take place on November 26, 2028. The announcement came exactly a year after the military seized power, having promised to restore civilian rule within 12 months.

The presidency said an assessment of preparations found insufficient technical, material and financial conditions to hold the polls as planned. It said the delay would allow time to ensure credible, transparent and inclusive elections with equal opportunities for all candidates. It also reaffirmed a commitment to the country's first-ever local government elections but gave no date.

The military overthrew President Umaro Sissoco Embalo in November 2025, three days after general elections and a day before provisional results were due. Both Embalo and challenger Fernando Dias had claimed victory. Embalo, now living in exile in Morocco, was barred from returning last month despite expressing interest in contesting the new elections. Guinea-Bissau has experienced numerous coups and attempted coups since independence from Portugal in 1974.

stories.headline: Venezuela to Repeal Law Barring Opposition Figures From Public Office
stories.summary:
Venezuela will repeal a law that bars opposition figures from holding public office, National Assembly speaker Jorge Rodriguez said. He expects the reform to be approved next week. The Simon Bolivar Law, passed shortly after the disputed July 2024 election, permanently banned anyone who requested or supported foreign sanctions from political office and allowed asset confiscation. Critics said it enabled political persecution, though Rodriguez said no politician had been subjected to its provisions.

Rodriguez, the older brother of interim president Delcy Rodriguez, said the law responded to a very specific moment. Her interim government has negotiated with opposition parties since taking over at the start of the year, when former President Nicolas Maduro was seized by the United States. Talks that began in August produced agreement on a review of several laws as part of a route map towards democracy, according to an opposition statement.

Delcy Rodriguez has promised free and fair elections but has set no date. Opposition leader Maria Corina Machado, who returned to Venezuela in October after more than 10 months in exile and was excluded from the transition talks, is widely expected to run if a vote is held. In 2024, the government-aligned electoral authority declared Maduro the winner without releasing detailed tallies, while the opposition said its ally Edmundo Gonzalez had won.
